title: Qronos: Correcting the Past by Shaping the Future... in Post-Training Quantization
claim: The overall procedure is a two-stage process: first transform inputs to be quantization-friendly, then round them onto a grid.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right, two chevron stages with math labels between
description: A single horizontal flow diagram with two large yellow chevron boxes labeled 'Stage 1: Transform' and 'Stage 2: Round'. On the far left, pre-trained weights and activations (W_orig^(l), X_orig^(l)) enter Stage 1 through a solid arrow. The output, transformed weights and activations (W^(l), X^(l)), passes through a second arrow into Stage 2. A dotted line comes from below, carrying X-tilde^(l), described as the potentially quantized input activations from the quantized model, and joins the arrow into Stage 2. The final arrow leads to the outputs Q^(l) and X-tilde^(l+1), the quantized weights and output activations. Text labels sit above and below each variable. The drawing is black on white with yellow boxes, and the eye goes to the two central chevrons first.
caption: The modern quantization pipeline is typically a two-stage process consisting of (1) transformations that make weights and/or activations more amenable to quantization, followed by (2) rounding functions that map weights and/or activations onto a quantization grid.
abstract: We introduce Qronos -- a new state-of-the-art post-training quantization algorithm that sequentially rounds and updates neural network weights. Qronos not only explicitly corrects errors due to both weight and activation quantization, but also errors resulting from quantizing previous layers. Our iterative algorithm is based on an interpretable and disciplined optimization framework that subsumes and surpasses existing data-driven approaches. At each step, Qronos alternates between error correction and diffusion via optimal update rules. Importantly, we prove that Qronos admits an efficient implementation that uses the Cholesky decomposition for solving least-squares problems. We also demonstrate that Qronos is compatible with existing transformation techniques such as Hadamard-based incoherence processing and weight-activation scaling equalization, among others. We evaluate Qronos using recent autoregressive language generation models in the Llama3 family; Qronos consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art adaptive rounding methods when quantizing the weights, activations, and/or KV caches.
